questions.q: What is −5 in 8-bit two's complement?
How many characters can 8-bit extended ASCII represent?
questions.why: 2⁸ = 256; standard ASCII uses 7 bits (128).

questions.q: Increasing the sampling rate of a sound file…
questions.why: More samples per second capture the sound more accurately.

questions.q: Run-length encoding of a bitmap image compresses:
o: Repeated characters in a text file
Runs of consecutive pixels of the same colour
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some described compressing a text file using characters instead of colours.

questions.q: How is the two's complement of a binary integer obtained?
o: Invert all bits (one's complement) and add 1
questions.why: Two's complement allows signed addition and subtraction with standard binary adder circuits: invert bits, then add 1.

long.q: Convert the denary number −45 into an 8-bit two's complement binary integer. Show your working.
scheme: M1: invert the bits: 11010010

long.q: A bitmap image is 1024 × 768 pixels with a colour depth of 24 bits. Calculate the file size in mebibytes (MiB), ignoring any header.
scheme: M1: 1024 × 768 × 24 bits, or × 3 bytes

long.q: Represent the denary number 2709 in packed binary-coded decimal (BCD) and give one application where BCD is used.
scheme: B1: an application, e.g. digital clock/calculator displays, or storing currency values so that decimal fractions are exact

long.q: One row of a black-and-white bitmap image is WWWWWWBBBWWWWWWWWBB, where W is a white pixel and B is a black pixel. Show how run-length encoding (RLE) would store this row, and explain why RLE is a lossless compression method.
scheme: B1: 6W 3B (first two runs correct)
B1: 8W 2B (last two runs correct)
B1: 19 pixel values are reduced to 4 count/colour pairs (8 values)
B1: lossless because no data is discarded, so the original row can be reconstructed exactly

long.q: The 8-bit two's complement integers 01011010 and 01001100 are added. Give the 8-bit result and explain what has happened.
scheme: B1: result 10100110
B1: overflow has occurred
B1: two positive numbers (90 + 76) give a negative result (−90) because the true answer 166 is outside the range −128 to +127

questions.q: Which topology connects every device to a central node?
questions.why: A failure of the central switch stops the network.

questions.q: What does CSMA/CD help with on a shared medium?
questions.why: Devices listen before sending and back off after a collision.

questions.q: Which is a characteristic, rather than a benefit, of a LAN?
o: It covers a small geographical area
Users can share files and printers
It gives every computer internet access
questions.why: Examiners (2023): there was confusion between benefits and characteristics, and 'a LAN gives internet access' was common.

questions.q: An IPv4 address is split into which two parts?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): 'Network IP and Host IP' instead of 'Network ID and Host ID' was a common error.

questions.q: Which protocol in the TCP/IP stack is responsible for resolving a domain name into an IP address?
questions.why: The Domain Name System (DNS) translates human-readable hostnames (e.g. panalo.app) into IP addresses.

long.q: Explain how CSMA/CD is used to manage the transmission of data on a shared Ethernet bus.
scheme: B1: a device listens to (senses) the bus and only transmits when it is idle
B1: while transmitting it monitors the bus to detect a collision (two devices transmitting at once)
B1: if a collision is detected, transmission stops and a jam signal is sent to all devices
B1: each device waits a random time before trying to retransmit

long.q: Compare the client-server and peer-to-peer network models.
scheme: B1: client-server: a central server provides resources/services that clients request
B1: client-server: security, backups and updates are managed centrally on the server
B1: peer-to-peer: no central server; every computer has equal status and can share its own resources
B1: peer-to-peer: cheaper and easier to set up but harder to manage security/backups, and performance depends on the peers

long.q: State two differences between IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, and explain why the devices on a home network are given private IP addresses.
scheme: B1: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits; IPv6 addresses are 128 bits
B1: IPv4 is written as four denary numbers separated by dots; IPv6 as eight groups of hexadecimal separated by colons
B1: private addresses cannot be routed on the internet, so the router uses NAT to share one public IP address between all devices
B1: this conserves the limited number of public IPv4 addresses / hides the internal devices from the internet

long.q: Describe how a web browser uses the Domain Name Service (DNS) to locate the web server for the URL a user types in.
scheme: B1: the browser extracts the domain name from the URL and sends it to a DNS server
B1: the DNS server looks up the domain name in its database/cache to find the matching IP address
B1: if it does not hold the entry, the request is passed to another (higher-level) DNS server
B1: the IP address is returned to the browser, which then sends its request to the web server at that address

long.q: A small company is considering moving all its file storage to a public cloud service. Evaluate this proposal by giving two benefits and two drawbacks.
scheme: B1: benefit, e.g. files can be accessed from anywhere with an internet connection / by many staff at once
B1: benefit, e.g. no need to buy and maintain its own servers; the provider handles backups and storage can be scaled up easily
B1: drawback, e.g. files cannot be accessed without an internet connection, or if the provider has an outage
B1: drawback, e.g. the data is held by a third party, raising security/privacy and legal concerns; ongoing subscription cost

questions.q: Which memory must be refreshed constantly?
questions.why: DRAM stores bits as charge in capacitors, which leaks.

questions.q: A logic circuit outputs 1 when exactly one input is 1. It is…
questions.why: XOR is exclusive OR.

questions.q: Which type of memory must be refreshed constantly?
questions.why: DRAM stores bits as charge in capacitors, which leaks away.

questions.q: For which inputs is X = (A NAND B) AND C equal to 1?
questions.why: A NAND B is 1 unless both A and B are 1, and C must also be 1; only A = 0, B = 1, C = 1 meets both conditions.

questions.q: A device's firmware must be updatable by the user downloading a new version, without removing the chip from the circuit board. Which memory should hold it?
questions.why: EEPROM can be erased and rewritten electrically while in the circuit; EPROM must be removed and erased with ultraviolet light, PROM can be written only once, and SRAM is volatile.

long.q: Describe two differences between static RAM (SRAM) and dynamic RAM (DRAM).
scheme: B1: SRAM uses flip-flops; DRAM stores bits as charge in capacitors
B1: DRAM must be refreshed regularly; SRAM does not
B1: SRAM is faster to access, so it is used for cache
B1: DRAM is cheaper per bit and denser, so it is used for main memory

long.q: A logic circuit has inputs A, B and C and output X = (A AND B) OR ((NOT B) AND C). Give the value of X for each input combination, in order from ABC = 000 to ABC = 111.
Describe how a laser printer produces a printed page.
scheme: B1: the drum is given an electrostatic charge
B1: a laser beam scans across the rotating drum, changing the charge to form an electrostatic image of the page
B1: charged toner is attracted to the parts of the drum holding the image
B1: the paper is charged and passes over the drum so the toner transfers to the paper
B1: a fuser unit heats and presses the paper to melt the toner onto it; the drum is then discharged for the next page

long.q: Explain the differences between PROM, EPROM and EEPROM.
scheme: B1: PROM can be programmed only once, after which its contents cannot be changed
B1: EPROM can be erased by exposure to ultraviolet light (chip usually removed from the circuit) and then reprogrammed
B1: EEPROM can be erased and rewritten electrically while still in the circuit, e.g. to update firmware

long.q: Explain why a buffer is used when a computer sends a document to a printer.
scheme: B1: the printer works much more slowly than the processor
B1: data is held temporarily in the buffer and the printer takes data from it at its own speed
B1: the processor is freed to carry on with other tasks instead of waiting for the printer

questions.q: In the fetch–execute cycle, what happens first?
o: The address in the PC is copied to the MAR
questions.why: MAR ← [PC]; then MDR ← memory; CIR ← [MDR]; PC incremented.

questions.q: Which addressing mode uses the operand as the actual value?
questions.why: Direct uses it as an address; immediate uses it as the value.

questions.q: Which describes the control bus?
o: It carries control and timing signals between components
questions.why: Examiners (2023): answers often said the control bus carries data or instructions; both are wrong.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the Program Counter (PC) in the Von Neumann architecture?
o: It counts how many programs are currently running
It holds the current instruction being executed
It holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched
questions.why: The PC points to the memory address of the next instruction; it is automatically incremented during the fetch phase.

questions.q: The accumulator holds 00010110. What does it hold after the instruction LSL #2?
questions.why: A logical shift left by 2 moves every bit two places left and fills the right with zeros, multiplying 22 by 4 to give 88 (01011000).

long.q: Describe the roles of the program counter (PC) and the memory address register (MAR) in the fetch stage of the fetch–execute cycle.
scheme: B1: the PC holds the address of the next instruction
B1: this address is copied to the MAR
B1: the instruction at the address in the MAR is fetched into the MDR (then CIR)
B1: the PC is incremented to point to the next instruction

long.q: Explain how increasing the width of the address bus and increasing the width of the data bus each affect a computer system.
scheme: B1: a wider address bus means more memory locations can be addressed
B1: e.g. each extra line doubles the addressable memory (n lines address 2ⁿ locations)
B1: a wider data bus means more bits are transferred at the same time
B1: so fewer transfers are needed per word/instruction, improving performance

long.q: Describe how the processor handles an interrupt.
scheme: B1: at the end of each fetch–execute cycle the processor checks for interrupts
B1: if an interrupt has a higher priority than the current task, the contents of the registers (including the PC) are saved on a stack
B1: the PC is loaded with the address of the interrupt service routine (ISR)
B1: the ISR is executed to deal with the interrupt
B1: the saved register contents are restored and the original task resumes

long.q: Memory addresses 200, 201, 205 and 206 hold the values 205, 17, 42 and 9 respectively, and the index register (IX) holds 1. Using the Cambridge assembly language instruction set, state the contents of the accumulator after each of these instructions is run on its own: (a) LDM #201 (b) LDD 200 (c) LDI 200 (d) LDX 200.
scheme: B1: (a) 201 (immediate: the operand itself is loaded)
B1: (b) 205 (direct: contents of address 200)
B1: (c) 42 (indirect: address 200 holds 205; contents of 205 loaded)
B1: (d) 17 (indexed: 200 + IX = 201; contents of 201 loaded)

long.q: The accumulator holds 10110110. Give its contents after each of these instructions, each starting from 10110110: (a) LSR #2 (b) AND #B00001111 (c) XOR #B11111111. Then explain the purpose of the mask in (b).
scheme: B1: the AND mask keeps the lower four bits unchanged and clears (sets to 0) the upper four bits, e.g. to isolate/test those bits

questions.q: Which is a benefit of an interpreter while developing code?
o: Errors are reported as each line runs, making debugging easier
questions.why: Compilers produce faster executables but report errors after compiling.

questions.q: Which is a utility program?
questions.why: Utilities help maintain the computer; others are applications or translators.

questions.q: What does a linker do?
o: Combines object code and library routines into one executable
Translates source code line by line
questions.why: A loader then copies the executable into memory.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of a program using a dynamic link library (DLL) rather than having the library code compiled into it?
o: The program can run even if the DLL file is missing
The executable file is smaller and the library can be updated without recompiling the program
The library code is copied into every program that uses it
The program can no longer have run-time errors
questions.why: A DLL is linked when the program runs, so its code is not stored in the executable and several programs can share one updated copy; the program fails if the DLL is missing.

questions.q: Which IDE feature lets a programmer run a program one statement at a time while checking the values of variables?
o: Single stepping with a variable watch window
questions.why: Single stepping runs one line at a time and a watch window shows variable values as they change, which helps locate logic errors; the others help while typing code.

long.q: Describe three key management tasks carried out by an operating system.
scheme: B1: memory management
B1: e.g. allocating memory to programs/processes and freeing it, keeping processes' memory separate
B1: file management
B1: e.g. organising files into directories, naming, saving, opening and setting access permissions
B1: a third task named, e.g. process management, hardware/peripheral management, security management, user interface
B1: a matching description, e.g. scheduling processes on the processor / communicating with devices through drivers / user accounts and passwords

long.q: Explain how disk defragmentation software can improve the performance of a computer with a magnetic hard disk.
scheme: B1: over time, files are saved in non-contiguous blocks scattered across the disk
B1: defragmentation moves the blocks of each file so they are stored together (contiguously) and groups free space together
B1: the read/write head moves less, so files are read and written faster

long.q: A programmer uses an interpreter while developing a program, then compiles it before selling it to customers. Explain why each translator is used at each stage.
scheme: B1: an interpreter stops at the first error and reports it, so errors can be found and fixed one at a time
B1: code can be tested without compiling the whole program / partly written programs can be run
B1: a compiled executable runs faster and does not need a translator on the customer's computer
B1: customers receive only object code, so they cannot see or easily copy/change the source code

long.q: Explain two benefits and one drawback of using dynamic link library (DLL) files.
scheme: B1: benefit, e.g. the executable file is smaller because the library code is not included in it
B1: benefit, e.g. one copy in memory can be shared by several programs / updating the DLL updates every program that uses it
B1: drawback, e.g. the program fails if the DLL is missing, or a changed DLL version is incompatible with the program

long.q: Describe three features of an IDE that help a programmer to find and correct errors in a program.
scheme: B1: breakpoints: the program stops at a chosen line so its state can be checked
B1: single stepping: the program is run one statement at a time
B1: a third feature, e.g. a variable/watch (report) window showing values as the program runs, or dynamic syntax checking that highlights errors as code is typed

questions.q: A firewall…
o: filters network traffic based on rules
questions.why: It allows or blocks traffic between networks.

questions.q: A check digit is used for…
questions.why: It is calculated from the other digits, e.g. ISBN.

questions.q: What does a firewall do?
o: Encrypts all data on a disk
Checks incoming and outgoing traffic against rules and blocks what is not allowed
questions.why: It sits between a network and the outside world.

questions.q: A hospital makes sure that only a patient's own doctors can view that patient's records. Which concept does this mainly protect?
questions.why: Data privacy means keeping personal data away from people who are not entitled to see it; integrity is about the data staying accurate and consistent.

questions.q: Which error would NOT be detected by a parity check on a byte?
o: Two bits changed in the same byte
The parity bit itself being flipped
Three bits changed in the same byte
questions.why: Changing two bits leaves the number of 1s odd or even as before, so the parity still matches; any odd number of changed bits is detected.

long.q: Explain the difference between data security, data privacy and data integrity.
scheme: B1: security: protecting data from loss, damage or unauthorised access
B1: privacy: keeping personal data confidential so it is seen only by those with the right/permission to see it
B1: integrity: making sure data is accurate, complete and consistent (unchanged by errors in entry or transmission)

long.q: A school system stores each student's date of birth. Describe two validation checks suitable for this field, explain why validation cannot guarantee that the data is correct, and name a method that would help.
scheme: B1: a check described, e.g. format check that the date matches DD/MM/YYYY, or presence check
B1: a second check described, e.g. range check that the student is aged between 11 and 19, or type check that it is a valid date
B1: validation only checks the data is reasonable/allowed, not that it is the true value (a wrong but valid date is accepted)
B1: verification, e.g. double entry or a visual check against the original document

long.q: Four bytes and a parity byte are received as a block: 01010011, 00110110, 11100101, 10001011, then parity byte 00000011. Even parity is used: the first bit of each data byte is its parity bit, and the parity byte gives even parity for each column. Identify the bit that is in error and give the corrected byte.
scheme: B1: byte 3 (11100101) has an odd number of 1s (five)
B1: column 5 (counting from the left) has an odd number of 1s
B1: the error is the bit where row 3 and column 5 meet
A1: corrected byte 11101101

long.q: Describe the difference between phishing and pharming, and give one way of protecting against each.
scheme: B1: phishing: a legitimate-looking email/message tricks the user into clicking a link or giving personal details
B1: pharming: malicious code on the computer or a DNS server redirects the user to a fake website even when the correct URL is typed
B1: protection against phishing, e.g. do not click links in unexpected emails; check the sender address; email spam filters
B1: protection against pharming, e.g. check the URL and the site's digital certificate; anti-malware software; secure DNS

long.q: Explain how a firewall helps to protect a network.
scheme: B1: it sits between the network and the internet and examines incoming and outgoing traffic
B1: it compares traffic against a set of rules, e.g. allowed IP addresses, ports or protocols
B1: traffic that does not meet the rules is blocked, preventing unauthorised access

questions.q: Open-source software…
o: makes its source code available to view and modify under a licence
is always free of all conditions
questions.why: Licences like GPL set conditions on sharing changes.

questions.q: Which statement about free software is correct?
o: Users may run, study, modify and share it; the source code is available
It is always free of charge but you cannot see the source code
It is the same as freeware
questions.why: Examiners (2023): there was confusion between freeware and free software.

questions.q: Which licence lets users study, modify and redistribute source code?
questions.why: Freeware is free to use but usually without the source code.

questions.q: A program can be downloaded and used free for 30 days, after which the user must pay to keep using it. Which type of licence is this?
o: Free software (as defined by the Free Software Foundation)
questions.why: Shareware is given out free for a trial period or with limited features, and the user pays to continue; freeware is free to use with no charge at all.

questions.q: A software engineer finds a safety flaw in a product, but her manager tells her to release it on time. Which principle of the ACM/IEEE Software Engineering Code of Ethics should guide her most?
o: Client and employer: always do what the employer instructs
Self: keep up to date with new technologies
Public: act consistently with the public interest
questions.why: Engineers must not release software that could harm the public, even when an employer asks; serving the employer has to be consistent with the public interest.

long.q: Explain why a computing professional should follow a code of conduct published by a professional body such as the BCS or IEEE.
scheme: B1: it sets standards of ethical behaviour, e.g. acting in the public interest and protecting the safety and privacy of users
B1: it requires competence and honesty, e.g. only taking on work they are qualified to do and being truthful with clients and employers
B1: following it maintains trust in the profession and the member's reputation; breaking it can lead to disciplinary action

long.q: Compare open source, shareware and commercial software licences.
scheme: B1: open source: the source code is available and users can study, modify and redistribute it
B1: open source: modified versions are usually distributed under the same licence terms
B1: shareware: free to use for a trial period or with limited features, after which a fee must be paid; no source code
B1: commercial: a licence must be bought before use; the software cannot be copied or modified and the source code is not provided

long.q: Explain why copyright legislation is needed for software, and describe two ways a software company can protect its software from being copied.
scheme: B1: software is expensive to develop but very easy to copy and distribute
B1: copyright law gives the creator legal rights over copying/distribution so they can earn from their work and take action against piracy
B1: one method, e.g. product keys/activation codes linked to a licence
B1: a second method, e.g. distributing compiled code only, online verification, digital watermarks or a dongle

long.q: A company replaces most of its human telephone customer-service staff with an artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot. Discuss the social, economic and environmental impacts of this decision. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: social: customers can get help 24 hours a day without waiting
B1: social: some customers, e.g. older people, may find a chatbot frustrating or unable to handle complex problems
B1: economic: lower running costs for the company as fewer staff are paid
B1: economic: job losses for call-centre staff, though new jobs are created in developing and maintaining the AI
B1: environmental: training and running AI uses large amounts of electricity in data centres
B1: environmental: fewer staff travelling to work / smaller offices can reduce emissions

long.q: A programmer finds a security flaw in her company's software. Her manager tells her not to mention it until after the product is launched. Describe how she should act ethically.
scheme: B1: she should put the public interest and the safety of users first
B1: she should report the flaw clearly and honestly to her manager in writing, explaining the risk
B1: if it is ignored, she should raise it through the proper channels in the company (more senior management) rather than leak it
B1: she should not knowingly approve or release software she believes to be unsafe

questions.q: A table is in 1NF when…
o: it has no repeating groups and every field is atomic
questions.why: 2NF removes partial dependencies; 3NF removes transitive ones.

questions.q: A foreign key…
o: uniquely identifies records in its own table
links to the primary key of another table
questions.why: It creates the relationship between tables.

questions.q: In a relational table, a tuple is:
questions.why: Examiners (2023): there was considerable confusion between rows and columns.

questions.q: In relational database design, what is a composite primary key?
o: A primary key that references a foreign key table
A primary key encrypted with a hash
A primary key formed by combining two or more attributes
questions.why: A composite key combines multiple columns to uniquely identify a record when no single column alone is unique.

questions.q: A table ORDER_LINE(OrderID, ProductID, Quantity, ProductName) has the composite key (OrderID, ProductID). ProductName depends only on ProductID. Which normal form does the table fail to meet?
o: None: it is already fully normalised
questions.why: ProductName depends on only part of the composite key, which is a partial dependency, so the table is in 1NF but not 2NF.

long.q: Explain what is meant by a foreign key, with an example from a school database with the tables STUDENT and CLASS.
scheme: B1: an attribute in one table that is the primary key of another table
B1: it is used to create a relationship between the two tables
B1: e.g. ClassID in STUDENT links to ClassID, the primary key of CLASS

long.q: Explain two limitations of using a file-based approach to store data, compared with a relational database.
scheme: B1: data redundancy: the same data is stored in several files
B1: this leads to data inconsistency when one copy is updated and others are not
B1: program–data dependence: programs are written for a particular file structure
B1: so changing the structure means rewriting programs; it is also hard to run new queries or control access to parts of the data

long.q: A shop stores order data in one unnormalised table: ORDER(OrderID, OrderDate, CustomerID, CustomerName, ProductID, ProductName, Quantity). One order can include many products; each customer and each product has one name. Normalise the data to third normal form (3NF), giving each table with its primary key.
scheme: B1: ORDER(OrderID, OrderDate, CustomerID) with primary key OrderID
B1: CUSTOMER(CustomerID, CustomerName) with primary key CustomerID
B1: ORDER_LINE(OrderID, ProductID, Quantity) with composite primary key (OrderID, ProductID)
B1: PRODUCT(ProductID, ProductName) with primary key ProductID
B1: foreign keys identified: CustomerID in ORDER; OrderID and ProductID in ORDER_LINE

long.q: Write an SQL statement to create a table BOOK with these fields: BookID (exactly 6 characters, the primary key), Title (up to 50 characters), Price (a real number) and InStock (true or false).
scheme: B1: CREATE TABLE BOOK( ... );
B1: BookID CHARACTER(6) (or CHAR(6))
B1: Title VARCHAR(50)
B1: Price REAL and InStock BOOLEAN
B1: PRIMARY KEY (BookID)

long.q: A hospital database has tables PATIENT(PatientID, PatientName, DoctorID) and DOCTOR(DoctorID, DoctorName, Ward). Write an SQL query to output the name of each patient and the name of their doctor, for doctors working on the ward 'Cedar', in alphabetical order of patient name.
scheme: B1: SELECT PATIENT.PatientName, DOCTOR.DoctorName
B1: FROM PATIENT INNER JOIN DOCTOR ON PATIENT.DoctorID = DOCTOR.DoctorID (or FROM PATIENT, DOCTOR with the matching condition in WHERE)
B1: WHERE DOCTOR.Ward = 'Cedar'
B1: ORDER BY PATIENT.PatientName (ASC)

questions.q: Abstraction means…
o: removing unnecessary detail to focus on what matters
questions.why: Decomposition, by contrast, breaks a problem into parts.

questions.q: FOR Count ← 1 TO 10 … NEXT Count. Which statement should not be inside the loop?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): FOR loops sometimes added an extra increment, so the loop ran the wrong number of times.

questions.q: What does a structure chart show?
o: The modules of a program, their hierarchy and the parameters passed
The data stored in a table
questions.why: Arrows show data and flags passed between modules.

questions.q: What is output? Count ← 0 ; FOR i ← 1 TO 10 ; IF i MOD 3 = 0 THEN Count ← Count + i ENDIF ; NEXT i ; OUTPUT Count
questions.why: Only i = 3, 6 and 9 are multiples of 3, and their values are added: 3 + 6 + 9 = 18. 3 would be how many multiples there are, not their sum.

questions.q: What is output? X ← 100 ; Steps ← 0 ; WHILE X > 1 ; X ← X DIV 2 ; Steps ← Steps + 1 ; ENDWHILE ; OUTPUT Steps
questions.why: X goes 100, 50, 25, 12, 6, 3, 1 (DIV discards the remainder), which is six passes; the loop then stops because 1 > 1 is false.

long.q: Write pseudocode for a function LinearSearch(Items, Target) that returns the index of Target in the 1D array Items[1:100], or −1 if it is not found.
scheme: M1: function header with parameters and RETURNS INTEGER
M1: a loop over indices 1 to 100
M1: compares Items[Index] with Target
M1: returns Index as soon as it is found
M1: returns −1 after the loop if not found

long.q: Explain what is meant by abstraction and by decomposition, using examples from the design of a program for a school library.
scheme: B1: abstraction: removing unnecessary detail to keep only what is needed to solve the problem
B1: example, e.g. a book is represented only by ISBN, title, author and loan status, not its colour or weight
B1: decomposition: breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems/modules that are easier to solve
B1: example, e.g. separate modules for adding members, issuing books, returning books and calculating fines

long.q: Trace this algorithm and state its purpose: Num ← 1734 ; Total ← 0 ; WHILE Num > 0 ; Digit ← Num MOD 10 ; IF Digit MOD 2 = 1 THEN Total ← Total + Digit ENDIF ; Num ← Num DIV 10 ; ENDWHILE ; OUTPUT Total
scheme: B1: Digit takes the values 4, 3, 7, 1
B1: Num takes the values 173, 17, 1, 0
B1: Total takes the values 0 (unchanged for 4), 3, 10, 11
B1: the output is 11
B1: purpose: adds up the odd digits of the number

long.q: Explain what is meant by stepwise refinement and give two reasons why it is used when designing a program.
scheme: B1: the problem is broken down into steps, and each step is repeatedly broken into more detailed steps until each can be coded directly
B1: reason, e.g. each small step is easier to understand, code and test
B1: second reason, e.g. different steps can be given to different programmers / modules can be reused

long.q: Write pseudocode for this algorithm, given in structured English: set Count to 0; input a value; while the value is not −1, add 1 to Count if the value is between 1 and 100 inclusive, then input the next value; finally output Count.
scheme: M1: Count ← 0
M1: INPUT Value before the loop
M1: WHILE Value <> −1 ... ENDWHILE
M1: IF Value >= 1 AND Value <= 100 THEN Count ← Count + 1 ENDIF
M1: INPUT Value as the last statement inside the loop, and OUTPUT Count after the loop

questions.q: A stack works on which principle?
questions.why: Last in, first out; a queue is first in, first out.

questions.q: Which abstract data type is first in, first out?
questions.why: A stack is last in, first out.

questions.q: An item is added to a circular queue that is not full. What changes?
o: All items move down one place
Only the rear pointer moves on (wrapping to the start if needed)
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many wrongly said existing contents must be moved.

questions.q: An empty stack has these operations applied: PUSH 4, PUSH 7, POP, PUSH 2, PUSH 9, POP. Which item is now at the top?
questions.why: POP removes the most recent item: 7 is removed, then 2 and 9 are pushed and 9 is removed, leaving 4 at the bottom and 2 on top.

questions.q: A node is deleted from the middle of a linked list held in arrays. What must change?
o: Every node after it is moved up one place in the array
The start pointer is set to null
The pointer in the previous node is changed to point to the node after the deleted one
Only the data item in the node is set to an empty string
questions.why: Linking the previous node past the deleted one removes it from the list without moving any data; the freed node is normally added to the free list.

long.q: A stack is held in a 1D array Stack[1:50] with a variable TopPointer (0 when empty). Describe how an item is pushed onto the stack.
scheme: B1: check whether the stack is full (TopPointer = 50)
B1: if full, report an error / do not add
B1: otherwise increment TopPointer by 1
B1: store the item at Stack[TopPointer]

long.q: Write pseudocode to declare a record type Book with fields ISBN (string), Title (string), Price (real) and OnLoan (Boolean), and then declare a 1D array Library to hold 500 Book records.
scheme: B1: TYPE Book ... ENDTYPE
B1: DECLARE ISBN : STRING and DECLARE Title : STRING
B1: DECLARE Price : REAL and DECLARE OnLoan : BOOLEAN
B1: DECLARE Library : ARRAY[1:500] OF Book

long.q: A bubble sort is used to put the array [5, 2, 8, 1, 4] into ascending order. Give the contents of the array after the first pass and after the second pass, state how many swaps are made in the first pass, and explain why the last element does not need to be compared in later passes.
scheme: B1: after pass 1: 2, 5, 1, 4, 8
B1: after pass 2: 2, 1, 4, 5, 8
B1: 3 swaps in the first pass
B1: the largest value has moved to the end after the first pass, so it is already in its correct position

long.q: A circular queue is held in the array Queue[0:7] with the variables FrontPointer, RearPointer and NumberInQueue. Describe how an item is removed from the queue.
scheme: B1: check whether the queue is empty (NumberInQueue = 0); if it is, report an error
B1: otherwise copy the item from Queue[FrontPointer]
B1: increment FrontPointer; if it goes past 7, set it back to 0 (wrap around)
B1: decrement NumberInQueue by 1

long.q: A linked list is held in the arrays Data[1:10] and Pointer[1:10], with StartPointer for the first node and FreePointer for the first unused node; a pointer value of 0 means null. Describe how a new item is inserted at the start of the list.
scheme: B1: check there is a free node (FreePointer <> 0); otherwise report that the list is full
B1: NewNode ← FreePointer and store the item in Data[NewNode]
B1: FreePointer ← Pointer[NewNode], so the free list starts at the next free node
B1: Pointer[NewNode] ← StartPointer, so the new node points to the old first node
B1: StartPointer ← NewNode

questions.q: A function differs from a procedure because it…
questions.why: Both can take parameters; only a function returns a value.

questions.q: In pseudocode, a function gives back its result with:
questions.why: Examiners (2023): OUTPUT was often used in place of RETURN.

questions.q: Which pseudocode extracts 3 characters starting at position 2 of Name?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): LEFT() was used where MID() was needed.

questions.q: What is output? PROCEDURE Double(BYREF X : INTEGER) ; X ← X * 2 ; ENDPROCEDURE ; Num ← 5 ; CALL Double(Num) ; CALL Double(Num) ; OUTPUT Num
questions.why: BYREF passes the variable itself, so each call changes Num: 5 becomes 10 and then 20. With BYVAL only a copy would change and 5 would be output.

questions.q: Name ← "Cambridge". What is returned by MID(Name, LENGTH(Name) - 3, 3)?
questions.why: LENGTH(Name) is 9, so MID starts at position 9 − 3 = 6 and takes 3 characters: i, d, g.

long.q: Write a pseudocode function CountVowels(Text : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER that returns the number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u, in upper or lower case) in Text.
scheme: M1: FUNCTION CountVowels(Text : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER ... ENDFUNCTION
M1: Count ← 0 before the loop
M1: FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Text) ... NEXT Index
M1: extracts each character with MID(Text, Index, 1) and converts it to one case with LCASE (or tests both cases)
M1: if the character is a, e, i, o or u (IF ... OR ... or CASE OF), Count ← Count + 1
M1: RETURN Count after the loop

long.q: Explain the difference between passing a parameter to a procedure by value and by reference, and describe one situation where passing by reference is needed.
scheme: B1: by value (BYVAL): a copy of the value is passed, so changes inside the procedure do not affect the original variable
B1: by reference (BYREF): the address of the variable is passed, so changes inside the procedure change the original variable
B1: situation, e.g. a procedure that must return more than one value to the caller, such as swapping two variables

long.q: The text file Scores.txt holds one integer per line, stored as a string. Write pseudocode to read every line of the file and output the total of all the integers.
scheme: M1: OPENFILE "Scores.txt" FOR READ
M1: Total ← 0 before the loop
M1: WHILE NOT EOF("Scores.txt") ... ENDWHILE
M1: READFILE "Scores.txt", Line inside the loop
M1: Total ← Total + STR_TO_NUM(Line)
M1: CLOSEFILE "Scores.txt" and OUTPUT Total after the loop

long.q: Explain the difference between a pre-condition loop and a post-condition loop, and state which is more suitable for repeatedly asking for a password until a valid one is entered.
scheme: B1: a pre-condition loop (WHILE ... ENDWHILE) tests the condition before the body, so the body may run zero times
B1: a post-condition loop (REPEAT ... UNTIL) tests the condition after the body, so the body always runs at least once
B1: a post-condition loop, because the password must be asked for at least once

long.q: Study this function: FUNCTION Mystery(S : STRING) RETURNS STRING ; DECLARE R : STRING ; DECLARE i : INTEGER ; R ← "" ; FOR i ← LENGTH(S) TO 1 STEP -1 ; R ← R & MID(S, i, 1) ; NEXT i ; RETURN R ; ENDFUNCTION. (a) State the value returned by Mystery("Code"). (b) State the purpose of the function. (c) Write a pseudocode statement that uses Mystery to output "Palindrome" if the string Word reads the same backwards.
scheme: B1: (a) "edoC"
B1: (b) it returns the string reversed
B1: (c) IF Mystery(Word) = Word THEN
B1: OUTPUT "Palindrome" ... ENDIF

questions.q: Which testing uses values at the edges of the valid range?
questions.why: Boundary data tests the limits, e.g. 0 and 100 for a percentage.

questions.q: A stub is used in testing to:
o: Stand in for a module that is not written yet, returning a simple value
questions.why: Examiners (2023): mistakes included calling stub testing integration testing or saying the dummy module 'checks' the program.

questions.q: Why is the waterfall model unsuitable when requirements may change?
o: Each stage is finished before the next, so going back is slow and costly
It is only for small programs
questions.why: Iterative and RAD models suit changing requirements.

questions.q: After release, a program is changed so that it works with a new version of the operating system. Which type of maintenance is this?
questions.why: Adaptive maintenance changes a program to cope with a changed environment such as new hardware, a new OS or new laws; corrective fixes bugs and perfective improves performance or features.

questions.q: Testers use their knowledge of the code to choose data so that every path through it is executed at least once. What type of testing is this?
questions.why: White-box testing uses the structure of the code to pick test data; black-box testing only compares inputs with expected outputs without looking at the code.

long.q: Compare the waterfall model and rapid application development (RAD) as approaches to developing a program.
scheme: B1: waterfall: each stage is completed and signed off before the next begins, in a fixed sequence
B1: waterfall: the client sees a working program only near the end, so changes to requirements are hard and costly
B1: RAD: prototypes are built quickly and improved in short cycles with constant client feedback
B1: RAD suits projects whose requirements are unclear or changing, but is less suited to large projects needing detailed documentation

long.q: A function accepts a whole-number age from 18 to 65 inclusive. Give an example of normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary test data for this function, saying what the expected result is for each.
scheme: B1: normal: any whole number from 19 to 64, e.g. 30, accepted
B1: abnormal (erroneous): e.g. 100, −5 or "twenty", rejected
B1: extreme: 18 or 65, the largest/smallest valid values, accepted
B1: boundary: values on each side of a boundary, e.g. 17 rejected and 18 accepted, or 65 accepted and 66 rejected

long.q: Describe corrective, adaptive and perfective maintenance, giving an example of each.
scheme: B1: corrective: fixing errors (bugs) found after the program is in use
B1: example, e.g. correcting a calculation that gives a wrong total
B1: adaptive: changing the program to meet new requirements or a changed environment
B1: example, e.g. updating it for a new operating system or a change in tax law
B1: perfective: improving the performance or usability of a program that already works correctly
B1: example, e.g. making a search run faster or improving the user interface

long.q: Explain the differences between syntax errors, logic errors and run-time errors, giving an example of each.
scheme: B1: syntax error: the code breaks the rules of the language and will not translate, e.g. ENDIF missing or a misspelt keyword
B1: logic error: the program runs but gives the wrong result, e.g. using < instead of <=
B1: run-time error: the program crashes while running, e.g. division by zero or an array index out of range

long.q: Describe the difference between white-box and black-box testing, and explain the purpose of stub testing.
scheme: B1: white-box testing uses knowledge of the code to choose test data that tests every path through it
B1: black-box testing checks only that the inputs give the expected outputs, without looking at the code
B1: stub testing: a simple dummy module (stub) is written in place of a module that is not yet finished
B1: the stub returns a fixed value or a message so the rest of the program and its structure can be tested

questions.q: Normalising a floating-point number…
o: gives the maximum precision for the mantissa size
questions.why: The first two mantissa bits differ (01 or 10), so no bits are wasted.

questions.q: Why are floating-point numbers normalised?
o: To give maximum precision and a unique representation
To use fewer bits for the exponent
questions.why: A normalised mantissa starts 01 (positive) or 10 (negative).

questions.q: More bits are given to the mantissa and fewer to the exponent. What happens?
questions.why: The mantissa sets precision; the exponent sets range.

questions.q: What happens if a calculation produces a positive floating-point number too small to be represented in the allocated bits?
questions.why: Underflow occurs when the magnitude of a non-zero value is closer to zero than the smallest representable non-zero float.

questions.q: A normalised floating-point number has an 8-bit two's complement mantissa 10100000 and a 4-bit two's complement exponent 0010. What is its denary value?
questions.why: The mantissa 1.0100000 is −1 + 0.25 = −0.75 and the exponent is 2, so the value is −0.75 × 2² = −3.

long.q: Normalise the floating-point number with an 8-bit two's complement mantissa 00010110 and a 4-bit exponent 0011, and state its denary value.
scheme: M1: mantissa 0.0010110, exponent 3
M1: shift mantissa left 2 places, exponent − 2
A1: mantissa 01011000, exponent 0001

long.q: Show how the denary number −5.75 is stored as a normalised floating-point number with an 8-bit two's complement mantissa and a 4-bit two's complement exponent.
scheme: M1: 5.75 = 101.11 in binary
M1: two's complement of the mantissa: 10100100
A1: exponent 0011, giving 10100100 0011

long.q: A floating-point format uses an 8-bit two's complement mantissa and a 4-bit two's complement exponent. Give the binary representation and the denary value of (a) the largest positive number and (b) the smallest positive normalised number.
scheme: B1: (a) mantissa 01111111, exponent 0111
B1: (b) mantissa 01000000, exponent 1000

long.q: Explain why the denary value 0.1 cannot be stored exactly as a binary floating-point number, and describe one problem this can cause in a program.
scheme: B1: 0.1 in binary is a recurring fraction (0.000110011…)
B1: only a fixed number of bits is available, so the value is truncated/rounded and only an approximation is stored
B1: problem, e.g. a test for equality fails (adding 0.1 ten times may not equal 1.0) or rounding errors build up over repeated calculations

long.q: A file of customer records uses random (direct) file organisation. Explain how a hashing algorithm is used to store and find a record, and how a collision can be dealt with.
scheme: B1: a hashing algorithm is applied to the key field, e.g. CustomerID MOD number of blocks, to give an address
B1: the record is written at that address in the file
B1: to find the record, the same algorithm is applied to the key and the record is read directly from that address
B1: a collision (two keys giving the same address) is dealt with by storing the record in the next free location or in an overflow area, which is then searched

questions.q: Which layer of TCP/IP routes packets between networks?
questions.why: IP at the Internet layer addresses and routes packets.

questions.q: Which protocol sends email from a client to a mail server?
questions.why: POP3 and IMAP retrieve email.

questions.q: What is true of packet switching?
o: All packets must take the same route
Packets may take different routes and are reassembled in order
questions.why: Circuit switching reserves a path for the whole communication.

questions.q: Which protocol keeps emails on the mail server so they can be read and organised from several devices?
questions.why: IMAP keeps the mailbox on the server and synchronises it, so every device sees the same messages; POP3 usually downloads and removes emails, and SMTP only sends mail.

questions.q: In the BitTorrent protocol, what is the role of a tracker?
o: It is a peer that holds the complete file and keeps uploading it
It is the file that contains all of the shared data
It is a router that gives torrent traffic priority
It is a server that keeps a record of which peers are sharing pieces of the file
questions.why: A tracker tells a new peer which other peers in the swarm hold pieces of the file; a peer with the whole file is a seed.

long.q: Describe the role of each of the four layers of the TCP/IP protocol suite when a web page is requested from a server.
scheme: B1: application layer: the browser uses HTTP(S) to form the request for the page
B1: transport layer: TCP splits the data into segments/packets, adds port numbers and sequence numbers, and makes sure delivery is reliable
B1: internet (network) layer: IP adds source and destination IP addresses and routes the packets between networks
B1: link layer: the packets are sent as frames over the physical network, using MAC addresses

long.q: Compare circuit switching and packet switching as methods of sending data across a network.
scheme: B1: circuit switching: a dedicated path is set up for the whole communication before any data is sent
B1: circuit switching: data arrives in order with no delay, but the bandwidth is reserved even when no data is being sent
B1: packet switching: data is split into packets that may take different routes and are reassembled at the destination
B1: packet switching: makes efficient use of the network and can route around faults, but packets may arrive out of order or be delayed

long.q: Explain how the BitTorrent protocol allows a large file to be shared between many users.
scheme: B1: the file is split into many small pieces
B1: a user downloads a torrent file holding details of the file and the address of a tracker
B1: the tracker identifies the peers in the swarm that hold pieces of the file
B1: pieces are downloaded from several peers at the same time
B1: as soon as a peer has a piece it can upload it to others, so seeds and leechers share the load and there is no single server bottleneck

long.q: Describe the roles of SMTP and IMAP when an email is sent by one user and read by another on two different devices.
scheme: B1: SMTP is used to send the email from the sender's client to their mail server
B1: SMTP is also used to transfer the email from the sender's mail server to the recipient's mail server
B1: IMAP is used by the recipient's client to retrieve the email from their mail server
B1: with IMAP the email stays on the server and changes are synchronised, so it can be read and organised on both devices

long.q: Explain how a router decides where to forward a data packet.
scheme: B1: the router reads the destination IP address in the packet header
B1: it looks up the address in its routing table to find the best next hop/network
B1: it forwards the packet to the next router (or the destination network), possibly choosing a route that avoids congestion; the hop count/TTL is reduced

questions.q: RISC processors typically have…
o: a small set of simple instructions, often executed in one clock cycle
questions.why: This suits pipelining; CISC has many complex instructions.

questions.q: Which is a feature of RISC processors?
o: Simple instructions of fixed length, suited to pipelining
questions.why: CISC has complex instructions that may take several cycles.

questions.q: What is a virtual machine?
o: Software that emulates a computer, running on a host system
questions.why: It lets one machine run another OS, at a cost in performance.

questions.q: A processor has a 5-stage pipeline, each stage taking one clock cycle. With no hazards, how many clock cycles are needed to complete 6 instructions?
questions.why: The first instruction finishes after 5 cycles and then one more completes every cycle, so 5 + (6 − 1) = 10 cycles; without pipelining it would take 30.

questions.q: In a JK flip-flop, J = 1 and K = 1 when a clock pulse arrives. What happens to the output Q?
o: It toggles to the opposite state
It becomes invalid, as in an SR flip-flop with both inputs at 1
questions.why: J = K = 1 makes a JK flip-flop toggle on each clock pulse, which removes the invalid state an SR flip-flop has when both inputs are 1.

long.q: Compare RISC and CISC processors.
scheme: B1: RISC has fewer, simpler instructions; CISC has many, more complex instructions
B1: RISC instructions are of fixed length and usually take one clock cycle; CISC instructions vary in length and take several cycles
B1: RISC has many general-purpose registers and only load/store instructions access memory; CISC has many addressing modes
B1: RISC suits pipelining and puts more work on the compiler; CISC needs more complex hardware (microprogrammed control unit) but shorter programs

long.q: Explain how pipelining improves processor performance, and describe the problem caused by a conditional branch instruction in a pipeline.
scheme: B1: the fetch–execute cycle is split into stages, e.g. fetch, decode, execute, memory access, write back
B1: different instructions are at different stages at the same time, so one instruction can finish every clock cycle
B1: when a branch is taken, the instructions already fetched after it are the wrong ones
B1: the pipeline must be flushed and refilled, wasting clock cycles

long.q: Use Boolean algebra to simplify X = A.B.C + A.B.C̄ + Ā.B.C, showing your working.
scheme: M1: A.B.C + A.B.C̄ = A.B.(C + C̄)
M1: C + C̄ = 1, so this gives A.B
M1: X = A.B + Ā.B.C = B.(A + Ā.C)
A1: = B.(A + C), i.e. X = A.B + B.C

long.q: Describe how an SR flip-flop stores one bit, explain the problem when S = 1 and R = 1, and explain how a JK flip-flop overcomes it.
scheme: B1: S = 1, R = 0 sets Q to 1; S = 0, R = 1 resets Q to 0
B1: S = 0, R = 0 keeps the previous value of Q, so one bit is stored
B1: S = 1, R = 1 is an invalid state: Q and Q̄ become the same / the next state is unpredictable
B1: in a JK flip-flop J = 1, K = 1 makes the output toggle on the clock pulse, so every input combination is valid (and it is clocked/synchronised)

long.q: Give two benefits and two limitations of using virtual machines.
scheme: B1: benefit, e.g. several different operating systems can run on one physical computer
B1: benefit, e.g. new or untrusted software can be tested safely because a crash only affects the virtual machine
B1: limitation, e.g. performance is slower than running directly on the hardware
B1: limitation, e.g. the virtual machine is complex to set up and needs a powerful host with large memory

questions.q: Paging is a memory management technique that…
questions.why: Processes are split into pages that map to physical frames.

questions.q: What does the lexical analysis stage of compilation do?
o: Removes comments and white space and turns the source into tokens
Checks grammar against the language rules
questions.why: Syntax analysis comes next.

questions.q: In paging, memory is divided into:
o: Fixed-size blocks called pages and frames
questions.why: Segmentation uses variable-size blocks.

questions.q: What is the value of the Reverse Polish expression 6 2 3 + * ?
questions.why: 2 and 3 are added first to give 5, then 6 × 5 = 30; each operator acts on the two values directly before it on the stack.

questions.q: A running process requests data from a disk and must wait for it. Which state does the process move to?
questions.why: A process waiting for an I/O event is blocked; when the data arrives it moves to ready, not straight back to running, and waits for the scheduler.

long.q: Explain how a process moves between the running, ready and blocked states.
scheme: B1: ready → running: the scheduler allocates the processor to the process
B1: running → ready: its time slice ends or a higher-priority process needs the processor
B1: running → blocked: the process has to wait for an event, e.g. input/output to complete
B1: blocked → ready: the event it was waiting for has happened
B1: a blocked process cannot go straight to running; it must first become ready

long.q: Explain how virtual memory works and what is meant by disk thrashing.
scheme: B1: part of secondary storage is used as if it were extra main memory
B1: pages of a process that are not currently needed are stored on disk and swapped into RAM when needed
B1: disk thrashing: pages are swapped in and out so often that the processor spends more time swapping than executing
B1: performance drops sharply (and the disk is in constant use)

long.q: An identifier is defined in BNF by: <letter> ::= A | B | C ; <digit> ::= 1 | 2 | 3 ; <id> ::= <letter> | <id><digit>. (a) State whether each of these is a valid <id>: A, B12, 3C, CC1. (b) Rewrite the rules so that an identifier is one or more letters followed by one or more digits.
scheme: B1: A is valid
B1: B12 is valid
B1: 3C is invalid because it must start with a letter
B1: CC1 is invalid because only one letter is allowed
B1: <letters> ::= <letter> | <letters><letter> and <digits> ::= <digit> | <digits><digit>
B1: <id> ::= <letters><digits>

long.q: Convert the infix expression (A + B) * (C − D) / E into Reverse Polish notation, then use a stack to evaluate it when A = 6, B = 2, C = 9, D = 5 and E = 4.
scheme: B1: starts A B + C D −
B1: whole expression A B + C D − * E /
M1: 6 2 + gives 8 and 9 5 − gives 4, each result pushed back on the stack
M1: 8 * 4 = 32 pushed on the stack

long.q: Describe what happens during the lexical analysis, syntax analysis and code optimisation stages of compilation.
scheme: B1: lexical analysis: whitespace and comments are removed
B1: lexical analysis: the code is split into tokens; keywords are identified and identifiers are added to the symbol table
B1: syntax analysis: the tokens are checked against the grammar rules of the language (e.g. a parse tree is built) and syntax errors are reported
B1: code optimisation: the code is changed so it runs faster or uses less memory, e.g. by removing redundant instructions

questions.q: A digital signature is created using…
questions.why: Anyone can verify it with the sender's public key.

questions.q: Data sent to Asha is encrypted with which key?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates confused public and private keys. Only Asha's private key can decrypt it.

questions.q: How is a digital signature produced?
o: The message is encrypted with the receiver's public key
The message is hashed and the hash is encrypted with the sender's private key
questions.why: Anyone can check it with the sender's public key.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a digital certificate?
o: To encrypt a message with a shared symmetric key
To store the user's private key on a public server
To confirm that a public key belongs to a named organisation, signed by a certificate authority
To compress data before it is transmitted
questions.why: A certificate authority signs the certificate to vouch that the public key in it really belongs to that organisation, so others can trust it.

questions.q: Bob receives a message with a digital signature from Asha. Which key does Bob use to decrypt the signature and check the message digest?
questions.why: Asha encrypted the digest with her private key, so only her public key decrypts it; if it matches Bob's own hash of the message, the message is authentic and unchanged.

long.q: Explain how asymmetric encryption is used to send a confidential message.
scheme: B1: the receiver has a public key and a private key
B1: the sender encrypts with the receiver's public key
B1: only the receiver's private key can decrypt it
B1: the private key is never shared

long.q: Describe how a digital signature is created by the sender, and how the receiver uses it to check who sent a message and that it has not been changed.
scheme: B1: the sender applies a hashing algorithm to the message to produce a message digest
B1: the digest is encrypted with the sender's private key to form the digital signature, which is sent with the message
B1: the receiver decrypts the signature with the sender's public key to recover the digest
B1: the receiver hashes the received message with the same algorithm
B1: if the two digests match, the message has not been altered
B1: because only the sender's public key decrypts it, the signature must have been made with the sender's private key, confirming the sender

long.q: Explain how an organisation obtains a digital certificate and state three items it contains.
scheme: B1: the organisation applies to a Certificate Authority (CA), sending its public key and proof of identity
B1: the CA checks the organisation's identity and issues the certificate, signed with the CA's private key
B1: contains, e.g. the owner's name and the owner's public key
B1: and, e.g. the serial number, validity dates, and the CA's name and digital signature

long.q: Describe how TLS sets up a secure connection between a web browser and a web server.
scheme: B1: the browser sends a hello message listing the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports
B1: the server replies with its choice of cipher and its digital certificate
B1: the browser checks the certificate with the CA's public key to confirm the server is genuine
B1: a session key is agreed using asymmetric encryption (e.g. encrypted with the server's public key)
B1: the rest of the session is encrypted with the shared session key using symmetric encryption

long.q: Give two benefits and two drawbacks of using quantum cryptography to send encryption keys.
scheme: B1: benefit: any attempt to eavesdrop changes the state of the photons, so it is detected
B1: benefit: keys can be exchanged with near-unbreakable security, and long keys can be used
B1: drawback: needs expensive specialist hardware and dedicated fibre-optic links
B1: drawback: limited range because the photons are lost or changed over long distances, causing errors

questions.q: Dijkstra's algorithm finds…
o: the shortest path from one node to the others
questions.why: A* extends it with a heuristic.

questions.q: What does Dijkstra's algorithm find?
o: The shortest path from one node to the others in a weighted graph
The largest number in a list
A spanning tree of equal weights
questions.why: A* adds a heuristic to guide the search.

questions.q: In supervised learning, the training data are:
questions.why: Unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabelled data.

questions.q: What distinguishes A* search from standard Dijkstra's algorithm?
o: A* uses an admissible heuristic function h(n) to estimate the cost to the goal
A* cannot find the shortest path
A* only works on trees with equal weights
questions.why: A* evaluates nodes using f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where h(n) is an admissible heuristic that never overestimates the distance to the goal.

questions.q: A program learns to play a game by being rewarded for good moves and penalised for bad ones. Which type of machine learning is this?
questions.why: Reinforcement learning improves by trial and error using rewards and penalties; supervised learning needs labelled examples of the correct outputs.

long.q: Describe how Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path between two nodes.
scheme: B1: set the start node's distance to 0 and all others to infinity
B1: repeatedly visit the unvisited node with the smallest distance
B1: update neighbours' distances if a shorter path is found
B1: stop when the destination is visited; trace back for the path

long.q: A graph has nodes A, B, C, D and E with these edges and weights: A–B 4, A–C 2, B–C 1, B–D 5, C–D 8, C–E 10, D–E 2. Use Dijkstra's algorithm to find the shortest distance from A to every node, and give the shortest path from A to E.
scheme: B1: C = 2 (direct from A)
B1: B = 3 via C (updated from 4)
B1: D = 8 via B (shorter than 10 via C)
B1: E = 10 via D (updated from 12 via C)
B1: path A → C → B → D → E

long.q: Explain how the A* algorithm differs from Dijkstra's algorithm, and why A* usually finds a route more quickly.
scheme: B1: A* adds a heuristic h(n), an estimate of the distance from each node to the goal
B1: it chooses the next node by the smallest f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g(n) is the distance from the start
B1: so it explores nodes leading towards the goal first and visits fewer nodes than Dijkstra's algorithm

long.q: Compare supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, giving an example application of each.
scheme: B1: supervised learning: the model is trained on labelled data, with the correct output given for each input
B1: example, e.g. classifying emails as spam or not spam / predicting house prices
B1: unsupervised learning: the model finds patterns or groups in unlabelled data
B1: example, e.g. grouping customers by buying habits
B1: reinforcement learning: an agent learns by trial and error, receiving rewards or penalties for its actions
B1: example, e.g. learning to play a game or control a robot

long.q: Describe the structure of an artificial neural network and explain how back propagation of errors is used to train it.
scheme: B1: an input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer of nodes (neurons)
B1: nodes in each layer are connected to the next layer by links with weights
B1: during training the network's output is compared with the expected output to find the error
B1: the error is passed backwards through the network from the output layer
B1: the weights are adjusted to reduce the error, and the process is repeated many times

questions.q: A binary search looks for 23 in the sorted array [3, 8, 12, 15, 19, 23, 30, 41, 56] with indexes 1 to 9, using Mid ← (Low + High) DIV 2. Which values are compared with 23, in order?
questions.why: Mid = 5 gives 19 (too small, so Low = 6); Mid = 7 gives 30 (too large, so High = 6); Mid = 6 gives 23, which is found.

questions.q: FUNCTION F(N : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER ; IF N = 0 THEN RETURN 0 ELSE RETURN N + F(N - 1) ENDIF ; ENDFUNCTION. What does F(4) return?
questions.why: F(4) = 4 + F(3) = 4 + 3 + F(2) … = 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 10; the calls unwind once the base case F(0) returns 0.

long.q: Write a pseudocode function BinarySearch(Target : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER that searches the global array Items[1:100], sorted in ascending order, and returns the index of Target, or −1 if it is not found.
scheme: M1: Low ← 1 and High ← 100
M1: WHILE Low <= High ... ENDWHILE (the loop ends when the search space is empty)
M1: Mid ← (Low + High) DIV 2
M1: IF Items[Mid] = Target THEN RETURN Mid
M1: if Items[Mid] < Target THEN Low ← Mid + 1
M1: otherwise High ← Mid − 1
M1: RETURN −1 after the loop

long.q: An insertion sort is used to put the array [7, 3, 9, 2, 5] into ascending order. Give the contents of the array after each of the four passes, and explain why insertion sort is efficient for data that is already nearly sorted.
scheme: B1: after pass 1: 3, 7, 9, 2, 5
B1: after pass 2: 3, 7, 9, 2, 5 (9 is already in place)
B1: after pass 3: 2, 3, 7, 9, 5
B1: after pass 4: 2, 3, 5, 7, 9
B1: each item needs few or no comparisons/moves when it is already near its place, so the time approaches O(n)

long.q: State the worst-case time complexity in Big O notation of a linear search, a binary search, a bubble sort and an insertion sort, and explain why a binary search is much faster than a linear search on a large sorted array.
scheme: B1: linear search O(n)
B1: binary search O(log n)
B1: bubble sort O(n²) and insertion sort O(n²)
B1: a binary search halves the number of items left to search with each comparison
B1: e.g. at most about 20 comparisons for 1 000 000 items, compared with up to 1 000 000 for a linear search

long.q: The values 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, 35 are inserted in that order into an empty binary search tree. Describe the tree, give its in-order traversal, and state how many nodes are compared when searching for 35.
scheme: B1: 50 is the root, with 30 as its left child and 70 as its right child
B1: 20 and 40 are the left and right children of 30; 60 and 80 are the left and right children of 70
B1: 35 is the left child of 40
B1: 4 comparisons (50, 30, 40, 35)

long.q: FUNCTION Power(B : INTEGER, E : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER ; IF E = 0 THEN RETURN 1 ELSE RETURN B * Power(B, E - 1) ENDIF ; ENDFUNCTION. Trace the call Power(3, 4), state the value returned, and explain why the base case is essential.
scheme: B1: calls Power(3, 4), Power(3, 3), Power(3, 2), Power(3, 1), Power(3, 0)
B1: Power(3, 0) is the base case and returns 1
B1: as the calls unwind they return 3, 9, 27
A1: Power(3, 4) returns 81
B1: without a base case the function calls itself forever until the stack overflows

long.q: Write pseudocode for a recursive function Factorial(N) that returns N!.

M1: correct ENDIF / ENDFUNCTION

long.q: Write pseudocode for a class Account with two private attributes, AccountNumber (STRING) and Balance (REAL); a constructor that takes an account number and sets Balance to 0; a getter GetBalance(); and a method Withdraw(Amount) that subtracts Amount and returns TRUE only if the balance is large enough, otherwise returns FALSE and leaves the balance unchanged.
scheme: B1: CLASS Account ... ENDCLASS
B1: PRIVATE AccountNumber : STRING and PRIVATE Balance : REAL
B1: PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(Number : STRING) with AccountNumber ← Number and Balance ← 0
B1: PUBLIC FUNCTION GetBalance() RETURNS REAL with RETURN Balance
B1: PUBLIC FUNCTION Withdraw(Amount : REAL) RETURNS BOOLEAN
B1: IF Amount <= Balance THEN Balance ← Balance − Amount and RETURN TRUE
B1: ELSE RETURN FALSE, with Balance unchanged

long.q: Explain what is meant by encapsulation in object-oriented programming, and why classes provide getter and setter methods.
scheme: B1: encapsulation: an object's attributes and the methods that act on them are combined in one class
B1: the attributes are made private so they cannot be accessed directly from outside the class
B1: getters and setters are public methods that give controlled access to read or change the private attributes
B1: a setter can validate the new value before it is stored, protecting the data's integrity

long.q: A declarative program holds these facts: flight(london, paris). flight(paris, rome). flight(rome, athens). flight(london, dublin). (a) Give the results of the goal flight(london, Z). (b) Write a rule connects(X, Y) that is true if there is a direct flight from X to Y or a journey with exactly one change. (c) State whether connects(london, rome) and connects(london, athens) succeed, with reasons.
scheme: B1: (a) Z = paris and Z = dublin
B1: (b) connects(X, Y) IF flight(X, Y)
B1: (b) OR flight(X, Z) AND flight(Z, Y), using an intermediate variable Z
B1: (c) connects(london, rome) succeeds (true), via paris
B1: (c) connects(london, athens) fails (false) because it needs two changes

long.q: Explain what is meant by an exception, and describe how exception handling could be used when a program opens and reads a file that might not exist.
scheme: B1: an exception is an unexpected event/error that occurs while a program is running
B1: the code that opens and reads the file is placed in a try block
B1: if an exception is raised, e.g. file not found, control passes to the matching except/catch block
B1: the handler deals with it, e.g. displays a helpful message or creates the file, so the program does not crash
